questions.prompt: After a WLAN policy change, all APs managed by one controller advertise a new network consistently. What did the controller contribute?

choices.text: Conversion of every client into a router
choices.explanation: Client forwarding roles need not change.

choices.text: Central coordination of WLAN configuration
choices.explanation: Managed AP policy can be distributed centrally.

choices.text: Replacement of radio transmission with TCP
choices.explanation: Clients still use an 802.11 radio link.

choices.text: Electrical power through the SSID
choices.explanation: SSID text does not deliver power.

questions.explanation: Central management reduces the need to configure each managed AP independently. The APs still provide the radio interfaces to clients.

questions.prompt: A basic fabric has four spines. A new leaf must connect once to every spine. How many additional leaf-to-spine links are required?

choices.text: Two

choices.text: Eight

choices.text: Four

questions.prompt: A switch port and server NIC operate at 1 Gb/s full duplex over a dedicated link. Which behavior is consistent with this connection?

choices.text: Both may transmit and receive simultaneously without Ethernet collisions
choices.explanation: Full duplex separates simultaneous transmission and reception.

choices.text: They must use CSMA/CD to schedule every transmitted frame
choices.explanation: Collision-based access applies to half-duplex Ethernet.

choices.text: The server shares one collision domain with every switch port
choices.explanation: The switch separates point-to-point links.

choices.text: Only one direction can carry traffic at a time
choices.explanation: That describes half-duplex behavior.

questions.explanation: A full-duplex point-to-point Ethernet link does not use collisions to arbitrate access. It can carry traffic in both directions concurrently.

questions.prompt: A copper link intended for 1 Gb/s negotiates at 100 Mb/s on both ends. A cable tester finds two usable pairs but faults on the other two; both ports support 1000BASE-T. What best explains the reduced rate?

choices.text: A DNS lookup selected a slower link
choices.explanation: DNS does not negotiate physical link speed.

choices.text: A mismatched subnet forces half duplex
choices.explanation: Subnet masks do not control Ethernet negotiation.

choices.text: The damaged pairs prevent the required four-pair gigabit operation
choices.explanation: 1000BASE-T requires all four pairs, unlike 100BASE-TX.

choices.text: 100 Mb/s proves all four pairs are intact
choices.explanation: A 100 Mb/s link can work while pairs needed for gigabit are faulty.

questions.explanation: The physical evidence identifies a cable capability problem. Matching operational speed on both ends means this is not an observed speed mismatch.

choices.text: A destination port field

choices.text: Connection establishment using SYN exchange

choices.text: The physical host loses power

questions.prompt: A crowded 5 GHz deployment changes channel width from 80 MHz to 20 MHz while retaining an appropriate channel plan. Which TWO effects are plausible? Select two.

choices.text: More separate nonoverlapping channels become available within the same spectrum
choices.explanation: Narrower channels consume less spectrum per channel.

choices.text: Every client must obtain a new IPv6 address
choices.explanation: RF width does not inherently force IPv6 renumbering.

choices.text: The SSID becomes hidden automatically
choices.explanation: Visibility is unrelated to channel width.

choices.text: Peak PHY rate per radio may decrease under comparable conditions
choices.explanation: Narrower bandwidth can reduce the achievable physical data rate.

choices.text: All external interference disappears
choices.explanation: Other transmitters and noise sources can remain.

questions.prompt: A dynamic MAC entry has a 300-second aging interval. Its source sends eligible frames every 60 seconds on the same port. With no topology changes, what should happen?

choices.text: The entry expires exactly 300 seconds after first learning
choices.explanation: Subsequent source observations refresh its age.

choices.text: The entry becomes a static configuration automatically
choices.explanation: Frequent traffic does not convert dynamic entries to static.

choices.text: The entry stays fresh while those source frames continue
choices.explanation: The timer is refreshed by relevant source traffic.

choices.text: The switch forgets all other entries on each refresh
choices.explanation: Refreshing one entry does not clear the entire table.

questions.explanation: Aging removes unused dynamic information. Regular source observations maintain the mapping rather than letting its original timestamp dictate expiration.

questions.prompt: The switch-to-router trunk carries native VLAN 88 untagged, with native tagging disabled. R1 should be the gateway for VLAN 88, but the shown subinterface expects tagged traffic. What change aligns the router with the existing trunk design?

exhibit.content:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.88
 encapsulation dot1Q 88
 ip address 10.88.0.1 255.255.255.0

choices.text: Place a VLAN 88 access command on the router’s routed subinterface.
choices.explanation: A routed subinterface uses dot1Q encapsulation, not switchport access membership.

choices.text: Change the subnet mask to /16.
choices.explanation: An IP mask does not repair a tagging mismatch.

choices.text: Rename the subinterface Gi0/0.1 without changing encapsulation.
choices.explanation: The suffix does not change frame classification.

choices.text: Use encapsulation dot1Q 88 native on Gi0/0.88.
choices.explanation: The native keyword binds untagged traffic to this router subinterface.

questions.explanation: The router and switch must agree on whether this VLAN is tagged. The dot1Q native keyword matches the stated untagged gateway design.

choices.text: The switch automatically merges both VLANs into one subnet.

choices.text: The PCs remain in separate Layer 2 broadcast domains.

choices.text: The switch converts both access ports into a trunk.
choices.explanation: Host addressing does not negotiate trunk mode.

questions.prompt: A maintenance engineer must remove VLAN 55 from a trunk without changing the allowed status of VLANs 15 and 35. Which command is appropriate?

exhibit.content:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/45
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 15,35,55

choices.text: switchport access vlan 15
choices.explanation: An access VLAN command does not edit an operational trunk’s allowed list.

choices.text: switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 55
choices.explanation: The remove form subtracts 55 while retaining the existing other entries.

choices.text: no vlan 55
choices.explanation: Deleting the VLAN is a switch-wide operation, not a scoped change to this trunk.

choices.text: switchport trunk allowed vlan 55
choices.explanation: This replaces the list with only VLAN 55, reversing the requirement.

questions.explanation: Modify the specific trunk policy instead of deleting a VLAN globally. The command’s add/remove semantics matter during incremental changes.

questions.prompt: A technician unplugs a discovered neighbor. Shortly afterward the old CDP entry is still displayed with a decreasing holdtime. No new advertisements arrive. What is the most reasonable interpretation?

choices.text: The displayed entry can remain until its hold timer expires.
choices.explanation: Discovery tables are cached and do not inherently prove a live connection at every instant.

choices.text: CDP proves the disconnected cable still forwards user traffic.
choices.explanation: A remaining cache entry is not current forwarding evidence.

choices.text: The holdtime is the Ethernet propagation delay.
choices.explanation: It represents remaining advertisement validity, not cable delay.

choices.text: CDP must be routed through the Internet from that neighbor.
choices.explanation: CDP discovers directly attached Layer 2 neighbors.

questions.explanation: Read cached discovery output alongside interface state and elapsed time. An aging entry can outlast the last received advertisement.

questions.prompt: The shown LACP configuration uses channel-group 3 on SW-A and channel-group 8 on SW-B. All other parameters and physical connections are compatible. Why can this still form one channel between the switches?

exhibit.content:
SW-A members: channel-group 3 mode active
SW-B members: channel-group 8 mode passive

choices.text: Only static mode on permits different group numbers.
choices.explanation: This local numbering principle also applies to LACP.

choices.text: Channel-group numbers identify local logical interfaces and need not match across peers.
choices.explanation: LACP uses its protocol identifiers and member compatibility, not equality of local CLI group numbers.

choices.text: Both switches automatically rename themselves to group 1.
choices.explanation: No such renaming is required or implied.

choices.text: The bundle must fail because the numbers become VLAN tags.
choices.explanation: Port-channel identifiers are not 802.1Q VLAN IDs.

questions.explanation: A channel-group number is locally significant. Verify actual negotiation and member compatibility instead of assuming peer numbering must be identical.

questions.prompt: Distribution A is configured with base priority 24576 for VLAN 10 and 28672 for VLAN 20. Distribution B uses 28672 for VLAN 10 and 24576 for VLAN 20. All other switches use 32768 and remain connected. Which root placement results?

choices.text: Both are simultaneously root for VLAN 10.
choices.explanation: A connected converged VLAN instance selects one root.

choices.text: B is root for all VLANs because it wins VLAN 20.
choices.explanation: Winning one instance does not override another instance.

choices.text: A is root for VLAN 10; B is root for VLAN 20.
choices.explanation: Rapid PVST+ compares bridge IDs separately in each VLAN instance.

choices.text: A is root for all VLANs because VLAN 10 is lower.
choices.explanation: The VLAN number does not make one instance control every other instance.

questions.explanation: Per-VLAN spanning tree allows intentional root distribution. The lower priority wins independently for each VLAN.

questions.prompt: SW-P and SW-Q share a segment for VLAN 70. SW-P’s root-path cost is 8 and SW-Q’s is 12; their root IDs agree. Which switch supplies the designated port on that segment?

choices.text: SW-P, because it advertises the lower path cost to the root.
choices.explanation: The better root information wins the designated-port election on that segment.

choices.text: Neither, because only root bridges have designated ports.
choices.explanation: Nonroot bridges also supply designated ports on downstream segments.

choices.text: SW-Q, because the larger cost gives it higher priority.
choices.explanation: Lower path cost is preferred.

choices.text: Both, because neither is the root bridge.
choices.explanation: A shared segment elects one designated port for the instance.

questions.explanation: Designated-port election chooses the best advertised path on each segment. It is not limited to ports on the root bridge.
